before: Most accidents involving rear-end collisions result in finding that the driver who crashes into the car in front of him or her is the person at fault. This usually stems from the lack of stopping in time or negligent behavior that leads to the crash. However, there are times when the driver in front is at fault because of his or her own negligent driving practices.

Jones, 236 Ga. 448 (1976)). This usually stems from the lack of stopping in time or negligent behavior that leads to the crash. However, there are times when the driver in front is at fault because of his or her own negligent driving practices.

before:
The driver who crashes into a car from behind is typically found at fault. However, there are certain times when liability clearly falls on the rear driver, such as when participating in the following driving practices:
  • Tailgating — When a driver fails to leave enough space between his or her vehicle and the vehicle in front, this could lead to a collision.
  • Distracted driving — Cellphones, eating food, listening to music too loudly and engaging in discussions with passengers can all lead to distracted driving which can cause a rear-end accident.
  • Driving under the influence — Drug and alcohol consumption alter a driver’s behavior that can lead to judgment and decision impairments that typically result in an accident.
  • Sudden acceleration — Any abrupt change in speeds can lead to a collision when the driver is not paying attention.
after:
Liability usually points to the rear driver when the evidence shows practices such as the following:
  • Tailgating — When a driver fails to leave enough space between his or her vehicle and the vehicle in front, this could lead to a collision. Georgia law prohibits following more closely than is reasonable and prudent (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-49).
  • Distracted driving — Cellphones, eating food, listening to music too loudly and engaging in discussions with passengers can all lead to distracted driving which can cause a rear-end accident.
  • Driving under the influence — Drug and alcohol consumption alter a driver’s behavior that can lead to judgment and decision impairments that can result in an accident.
  • Sudden acceleration — Any abrupt change in speeds can lead to a collision when the driver is not paying attention.

In Georgia, modified comparative negligence rules apply. Under these rules, if you are less than 50 percent responsible for the accident, your damages will be reduced by your own percent of fault. Any level higher than this, and the injured party will not receive any compensation for the claim.

His or her level of damages is reduced by his or her own degree of fault. For example, if the insurance company or jury finds that the plaintiff was 20 percent at fault and the plaintiff sustained $100,000 in damages, his or her award would be reduced by $20,000.
after: In Georgia, modified comparative negligence applies (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33). If you are less than 50 percent responsible for the accident, your damages are reduced by your percentage of fault. At 50 percent or more, you recover nothing. For example, if a jury finds that the plaintiff was 20 percent at fault and the plaintiff sustained $100,000 in damages, his or her award would be reduced by $20,000, to $80,000. Insurers apply the same arithmetic in settlement talks.
